name: Bovine colostrum
short: Preterm infants: 2025 review of 4 trials found adverse-event data limited and benefit unproven, and did not recommend it; a pilot trial saw temporary raised tyrosine. Few adult safety data.
text: Safety data on bovine colostrum are limited. In preterm infants, a 2025 meta-analysis of four randomised trials (670 infants) found no significant effect on necrotising enterocolitis, said the evidence on adverse events was limited, and concluded that bovine colostrum cannot be recommended for preterm infants on current evidence; the same conclusion says the lower incidence of feeding intolerance seen with bovine colostrum is likely due to performance bias (the included trials lacked blinding), with no proven benefit for necrotising enterocolitis or time to full enteral feeding; an earlier meta-analysis of eight trials (385 infants) of human or bovine colostrum found no effect, compared with placebo, on severe necrotising enterocolitis, death, culture-proven sepsis or feed intolerance. In an open-label pilot safety trial in 40 preterm infants, 8 infants fed bovine colostrum had a temporary rise in plasma tyrosine on day 7, against 2 in the comparison groups, with no differences in feeding intolerance or clinical adverse events; the authors said a larger trial is needed to test safety. In adults, a randomised placebo-controlled trial of a colostrum protein supplement in 90 adults with moderate digestive discomfort (a 4-week run-in followed by 8 weeks of supplementation; 83 analysed) reported that it was well tolerated with an acceptable safety profile, and in an 8-week randomised trial in 29 rugby players, reported illness was not affected compared with soy protein. A 90-day study in rats of a filtered colostrum product given by mouth found no treatment-related adverse effects, and laboratory tests found no genetic toxicity. None of the cited abstracts addresses people with cow's milk allergy. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
